title: Sharding and partitioning
scopeHtml: Scope: range, hash, directory partitioning, shard key choice, cross-shard queries. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: Why shard
notes.html:
Sharding (partitioning) splits one big dataset across many machines, each holding a slice. Replication copies the same data; sharding divides different data. You shard when data or write volume exceeds one machine.

Triggers (rough numbers): a single database over 2 to 5 TB, write rate beyond what one primary can fsync (around 10k to 50k simple writes/s depending on hardware), or working set no longer fitting in RAM.

Worked example. 6 TB of orders, 20,000 writes/s peak. One Postgres node tops out near 8,000 writes/s with that data size. 4 shards: 1.5 TB and 5,000 writes/s each, with headroom.

Decision gravity. Sharding is the biggest one-way door in data architecture: every query, join, transaction and migration changes. Exhaust cheaper steps first: indexes, caching, read replicas, bigger machine, archive old data. Instagram, Notion and Figma all sharded Postgres only after years of single-node growth.

Industry examples. Instagram sharded Postgres by user id with logical shards mapped to physical servers. Vitess shards MySQL for YouTube and Slack. MongoDB and Cassandra shard natively.

Everyday analogy. A library too big for one building: books A-H in building 1, I-P in building 2. Finding a book is easy if you know the rule, awful if you need all the books about "ships".

Common interview traps.

  • Sharding at 50 GB. Premature, and permanent.
  • Confusing sharding with replication, or saying you shard "for availability".

notes.title: Range partitioning
notes.html:
Each shard owns a continuous range of the key. Shard 1: A to F, shard 2: G to M, and so on. Or by date: January in one partition, February in the next.

Strengths: range scans are cheap (WHERE created_at BETWEEN ... touches one or two shards) and ordering is preserved. Weakness: hot spots. If keys are sequential (timestamps, auto-increment ids), all new writes go to the last range.

Shard A: user_id 0        .. 25,000,000
Shard B: user_id 25,000,001 .. 50,000,000
Shard C: user_id 50,000,001 .. 75,000,000   <- all new signups land here

Worked example. Time-series metrics partitioned by day: today's partition gets 100% of writes (say 50k/s) while 29 older partitions sit idle. Fix: prefix the key with a bucket (sensor_id then time) so writes spread over sensors, while a single sensor's range is still contiguous.

Industry examples. HBase and Bigtable use range-partitioned tablets that split automatically when they grow; Postgres declarative partitioning PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at) is common for logs and archiving (drop an old partition instantly instead of a huge DELETE). Spanner and CockroachDB are range-based with automatic splits.

CREATE TABLE events (id bigint, created_at timestamptz, payload jsonb)
  PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at);
CREATE TABLE events_2026_11 PARTITION OF events
  FOR VALUES FROM ('2026-11-01') TO ('2026-12-01');

Decision gravity. Choose for range queries and time-based retention. Alternative: hash. Breaks with monotonic keys. Re-splitting ranges is reversible if the system splits automatically (Bigtable), painful if you hand-managed it.

Everyday analogy. A dictionary split into volumes A-C, D-F and so on: great for looking up all words starting "pre", but everyone writing new words for "Z" crowds one volume.

Common interview traps.

  • Range partitioning on timestamp for a write-heavy table.
  • Ignoring skew in the key (more surnames starting with S than Q).

notes.title: Hash partitioning
notes.html:
Compute hash(key) and map it to a shard. A good hash spreads keys evenly, so no hot range, but neighbouring keys end up on different shards, so range scans touch every shard.

Two ways to map hash to shard:

  • Modulo: shard = hash(key) % N. Dead simple, but changing N moves almost every key (going 4 to 5 shards relocates about 80% of data).
  • Consistent hashing / fixed slots: place shards and keys on a ring (or divide hash space into many fixed slots, for example Redis Cluster's 16,384 slots, and assign slots to nodes). Adding a node moves only about 1/N of the keys.

Worked example. 4 shards with modulo: key hash 17 goes to shard 1. Add a fifth shard: 17 % 5 = 2, so it moves. Of 100M keys, about 80M move, a night of heavy copying. With 16,384 slots, adding a node moves only the slots handed over (about 3,277 slots, 20%).

Virtual nodes. A physical node owns many ring positions (for example 256 vnodes) so load is smooth and a failed node's data spreads over many peers instead of doubling one neighbour. Cassandra defaults changed from 256 to a lower vnode count in newer versions (confirm in docs).

# Redis Cluster: slots 0-16383 divided among 3 masters
# node A: 0-5460, node B: 5461-10922, node C: 10923-16383
cluster-enabled: yes
cluster-node-timeout: 15000

Industry examples. DynamoDB and Cassandra (hash of partition key, ring), Redis Cluster (slots), MongoDB hashed shard keys, Memcached clients with consistent hashing.

Decision gravity. Chosen when access is mostly by key and load balance matters. Breaks for range queries and for one celebrity key (hash cannot split a single key). Choosing slots up front (many more than machines) keeps this reversible.

Everyday analogy. Dealing a deck of cards to players: everybody gets a fair mix, but you cannot hand out "all hearts in order" to one player.

Common interview traps.

  • hash % N with no plan for resizing.
  • Believing hashing fixes hot keys; one viral key still lands on one shard.

notes.title: Directory-based partitioning
notes.html:
A lookup table (the directory) says which shard owns each key or key group. Instead of a formula, you store the mapping: tenant 7 -> shard 3.

Strengths: total flexibility. You can move one big tenant alone, give VIP customers their own hardware, and rebalance without changing a hash function. Weakness: the directory is a critical dependency; it must be fast (cached), highly available and consistent.

Worked example. SaaS with 20,000 tenants. Mapping table has 20,000 rows (tiny, cached in each app server with 60 s TTL and invalidation on change). Tenant "BigCorp" uses 40% of the load, so it gets shard 9 alone; everyone else is spread over shards 1 to 8.

A common compromise is logical shards: hash the key into, say, 1,024 logical shards, and keep a small directory mapping logical shard to physical server. Moving one logical shard is a small, targeted copy. Instagram used this approach.

CREATE TABLE shard_map (
  tenant_id bigint PRIMARY KEY,
  shard_id  int NOT NULL,
  state     text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ACTIVE'  -- ACTIVE, MIGRATING
);

Industry examples. Vitess (VSchema and topology server), Slack's workspace-to-shard mapping, Salesforce multi-tenant orgs, Figma's and Notion's logical shard to physical database maps.

Decision gravity. Most flexible, so best for B2B multi-tenant data; the cost is an extra hop and a new service to keep alive. Reversible, as you can always change entries.

Everyday analogy. A hotel front desk keeping a list "guest X is in room 412" rather than assigning rooms by alphabet.

Common interview traps.

  • Making the directory a single point of failure or an uncached per-request lookup.
  • Forgetting to describe how the directory is updated safely during a migration.

notes.title: Choosing a shard key
notes.html:
The shard key is the column that decides where a row lives. It is the most important and least reversible choice.

A good key has:

  1. High cardinality (millions of distinct values, not 5 countries).
  2. Even distribution of load, not just of rows.
  3. Present in most queries, so each query hits one shard.
  4. Stable (changing it means moving the row).

Examples:

System Good key Bad key Why
Chat messages conversation_id message timestamp Timestamp is hot-tail
E-commerce orders customer_id order_status Status has 5 values, skewed
Multi-tenant SaaS tenant_id country A few huge countries
Social posts author_id (with care) post_id auto-increment Sequential hot shard

Worked example. Orders sharded by customer_id: "show my orders" hits 1 shard (5 ms). "All orders today for the CFO report" hits 16 shards, merges them: 80 ms and 16 times the load. That second query should go to a warehouse, not production shards.

Compound keys. Use (tenant_id, user_id) or add a random suffix (salting) for hot entities. Cassandra's partition key plus clustering key is exactly this: the partition key picks the node, clustering key orders rows inside.

Industry examples. Instagram: user id embedded in 64-bit ids (41 bits time, 13 bits shard id, 10 bits sequence), so any id tells you its shard. Twitter Snowflake ids are time-sortable. Uber's schemaless/Docstore shard by entity uuid.

Decision gravity. One-way door: resharding to a new key means rewriting all data and every query. Design the key from the top 3 queries, not from the table shape.

Everyday analogy. Sorting mail into pigeonholes by street name versus by "first letter of house colour"; the second rule is useless to the postman.

Common interview traps.

  • Choosing a key that matches the schema but not the access pattern.
  • Low-cardinality keys (country, boolean flags).
  • Forgetting that unique constraints and foreign keys only work within a shard.

notes.title: Cross-shard queries, joins and transactions
notes.html:
Once data is split, anything that touches more than one shard gets harder and slower.

Options:

  • Scatter-gather: ask every shard, merge results. Latency = slowest shard (p99 of N shards is much worse than p99 of one). With 16 shards each having a 1% chance of a slow response, about 15% of requests hit at least one slow shard.
  • Denormalize / co-locate: keep related rows on the same shard (orders and order_items both sharded by customer_id). Joins stay local.
  • Global/reference tables: copy small, rarely changing tables (countries, currencies) to every shard.
  • Secondary index tables: a second table sharded by a different key (email to user_id), maintained asynchronously or transactionally.
  • Analytics elsewhere: stream changes to a warehouse (see warehouses note).

Cross-shard transactions.

  • Two-phase commit (2PC): a coordinator asks all participants to prepare, then commit. Correct but blocks if the coordinator dies, and is slow.
  • Saga: sequence of local transactions with compensating actions (refund if shipping fails). Eventually consistent, no locks.
  • Better: design so one business transaction stays inside one shard.
Pagination across shards: ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 20 OFFSET 1000
Each shard must return its top 1020, coordinator merges and discards.
Deep offsets cost shards x offset rows. Use keyset pagination (WHERE id < last_seen).

Worked example. Fan-out count query across 32 shards where each shard answers in 10 ms median, 200 ms p99: the fan-out call's median is closer to the per-shard p90, around 40 to 60 ms, and its p99 is dominated by the worst shard.

Industry examples. Vitess handles scatter queries and offers vindexes for secondary lookup; CockroachDB and Spanner do distributed transactions with consensus per range plus 2PC across ranges; Citus (Postgres) uses co-located distributed tables and reference tables; Elasticsearch scatter-gathers every query by design.

Decision gravity. Accept cross-shard queries only for rare admin or reporting paths. If core user flows need them, the shard key is wrong.

Everyday analogy. Counting everybody's savings across 16 banks: you must phone each bank and wait for the slowest one.

Common interview traps.

  • Proposing 2PC casually; explain its blocking and latency costs.
  • Offset pagination across shards.
  • Assuming auto-increment ids, uniqueness and foreign keys work globally.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Shard only when one machine cannot hold the data or write rate; it is a one-way door.
  • Range: ordered, great for scans, hot-spots on sequential keys. Hash: even load, no scans; use many fixed slots or consistent hashing, not % N.
  • Directory: flexible mapping table (or logical to physical shards); must be cached and highly available.
  • Shard key: high cardinality, even load, in most queries, stable. Derive it from the top queries.
  • Cross-shard work is expensive: co-locate data, denormalize, reference tables, secondary indexes, sagas over 2PC, analytics in a warehouse.
